characters: Serwaa: a bright, determined Ghanaian girl introduced at age fourteen in JHS 2 in Kumasi (wearing a neat teal-and-khaki school uniform, glasses and natural braided hair) and later shown as a young mechanical engineer in her twenties wearing a teal work shirt and safety goggles.
Auntie Afia: Serwaa’s aunt, a hard-working tomato trader in Kumasi in her forties, wearing a warm gold-and-green wax-print cloth and head-tie.
Kojo: Serwaa’s classmate and later co-founder, an electronics enthusiast wearing spectacles and a navy polo shirt.
Mr Ofori: their JHS science and design teacher, wearing a cream short-sleeved shirt.

narrationPlan.voice: Confident, inspiring Ghanaian narrator (en-GH); earnest and analytical for Serwaa, warm for Auntie Afia and Mr Ofori.
narrationPlan.pace: Medium (about 125 words per minute); clear articulation of the valuation arithmetic on page 11.
notes: Pronounce Kumasi ("koo-MAH-see"), Serwaa ("sehr-WAAH") and Afia ("ah-FEE-ah") naturally.

music: Optional subtle acoustic guitar and light marimba pulse; off by default.
culturalNotes: Post-harvest tomato spoilage between farming hubs and Kumasi markets is a well-known agricultural challenge in Ghana.
Celebrates young Ghanaian women in STEM and engineering leadership.
reviewQuestions: Is the distinction between company valuation on paper and liquid cash clear to JHS learners?
Does the story clearly state that billion-dollar enterprises are rare exceptions while honouring businesses of all sizes?

pages.brief: Warm Kumasi market stall at late afternoon: Serwaa (14, glasses, braided hair, teal-and-khaki uniform) and Auntie Afia (gold-and-green wax-print dress and head-tie) looking thoughtfully at wooden crates of fresh red tomatoes beside a basket of bruised, overripe tomatoes.
pages.narration: Empathetic, grounded opening. Let Auntie Afia’s sigh carry real weight.

pages.brief: Sunlit Ghanaian JHS science classroom: Serwaa raising her hand at her desk while Mr Ofori (cream shirt) gestures toward a simple diagram of crates and a sun icon on a chalkboard (no readable text).
pages.narration: Thoughtful and inspiring tone from Mr Ofori.

pages.narration: Energetic curiosity, building to a suspenseful pause at the end.

pages.narration: Steady, mature progression showing years of disciplined study and engineering.

pages.narration: Warm triumph as the engineering solves the real-world market problem.

pages.brief: Modest startup office in Kumasi: Serwaa and Kojo looking at a wall map of Ghana marked with colourful pins and engineering blueprints rolled out on a wooden table.
pages.narration: Clear transition from engineering a product to scaling a company.

pages.narration: Serious, professional tone emphasising legal care and responsible ownership.

pages.brief: Clean modern assembly workshop in Ghana: Serwaa in safety goggles walking beside young Ghanaian male and female technicians assembling teal-and-silver solar cold-storage panels.
pages.narration: Dynamic, resilient tone highlighting local manufacturing and job creation.

pages.brief: Back in the Kumasi JHS classroom: adult Serwaa smiling warmly at a group of eager JHS students in uniform, holding a piece of chalk beside the board.
pages.narration: Playful question from the student, warm and grounded response from Serwaa.

pages.brief: Serwaa illustrating on the chalkboard with simple icons (a factory, solar panels, a delivery truck, and smiling workers, no words or numbers) while JHS students nod in understanding.
pages.narration: Crucial educational clarity: distinguish paper valuation and productive assets from personal cash, and note that such outcomes are rare.

pages.brief: Sunny school courtyard in Kumasi: Serwaa, Kojo, Mr Ofori and Auntie Afia smiling proudly as JHS students test small solar-powered models on a table.

teacherGuide.overview: A realistic JHS entrepreneurship and engineering story showing how a Ghanaian student team moves from observing post-harvest food loss in Kumasi to building prototypes, studying engineering, raising equity investment, creating local manufacturing jobs, and understanding the difference between paper valuation and cash.
learningGoals: Explain how iterative prototyping and engineering data turn early failures into working solutions.
Define prototype, scale, capital, equity and company valuation accurately.
Calculate company valuation from share count and share price (10,000,000 × 100 = 1,000,000,000 cedis) and distinguish it from personal cash.
Recognise that billion-dollar outcomes are rare exceptions, while businesses of every size succeed by creating value and decent jobs.
beforeReading: Preview the title and cover illustration with learners and ask what real-world problem or question the characters might face.
whileReading: Pause at the embedded comprehension and vocabulary activities to check understanding and discuss the evidence in the text.
afterReading: Problem-Spotter Walk: In pairs, list three everyday problems in your school or community (e.g., food spoilage, water waste, broken desks) and sketch a simple prototype that could help.

Valuation vs Cash Maths: Calculate the valuation of a fictional company with 50,000 shares priced at 20 cedis per share (1,000,000 cedis). If the founder owns 40% of the shares (20,000 shares), what is the paper value of their shares (400,000 cedis), and why can they not spend all of it at once without selling part of the company?
discussion: Why did Mr Ofori say great businesses start by solving a painful problem rather than simply wishing to become rich?
When the first coconut-husk prototype failed, what did Serwaa do differently from giving up?
Why did Serwaa and Kojo consult a corporate lawyer and an accountant before accepting investor money for equity?
If a company has 10 million shares valued at 100 cedis each, where does that 1 billion cedis of value actually sit?
reflection: If a company has 10 million shares valued at 100 cedis each, where does that 1 billion cedis of value actually sit?

whatWeKnow: Post-harvest loss is a major challenge for perishable crops in warm climates, and solar-powered cold storage with thermal energy storage is a proven engineering solution.

A company’s market valuation equals its total issued shares multiplied by the current price per share, representing enterprise ownership value rather than liquid cash in a founder’s personal bank account.
Equity financing exchanges partial ownership of a company for growth capital.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Engineers across Africa are actively researching cheaper, locally sourced phase-change materials and natural refrigerants to cut the cost of off-grid cold rooms even further.

investigation.title: Hands-On Insulation Challenge: Keeping Ice Cool
materials: Two identical small plastic cups, two ice cubes of equal size, dry coconut fibre or folded newspaper, a cloth wrap, and a watch or timer.
steps: Wrap Cup A snugly in dry coconut fibre or thick folded paper and cloth (your insulated prototype), and leave Cup B unwrapped in the shade.
Place one ice cube of the same size into each cup and cover both cups with a small card lid.
After 30 minutes, pour the melted water from each cup into a measuring spoon to see which cup slowed heat transfer better.

pronunciation.guidance: Ghanaians often say "uh-KRAH" (stress on the second syllable).

reviewerNotes: Confirm first-syllable stress and final vowel.
